claim: C. elegans has a compact nervous system containing a few hundred neurons.
source: C. elegans has a compact nervous system containing a few hundred neurons, for which a nearly complete wiring diagram of synaptic connectivity has been mapped (White et al., 1986; Varshney et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to White et al., 1986 and Varshney et al., 2011, which are foundational references for C. elegans neuroscience.

claim: A nearly complete wiring diagram of synaptic connectivity has been mapped for C. elegans.
source: C. elegans has a compact nervous system containing a few hundred neurons, for which a nearly complete wiring diagram of synaptic connectivity has been mapped (White et al., 1986; Varshney et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to White et al., 1986 and Varshney et al., 2011.

claim: C. elegans' optical transparency allows researchers to monitor neural activity with genetically encoded calcium and voltage sensors.
source: Worms' optical transparency allows researchers to monitor neural activity with genetically encoded calcium and voltage sensors (Kerr et al., 2000; Kerr, 2006; Flytzanis et al., 2014), and manipulate neurons and muscles using optogenetics (Nagel et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2007; Leifer et al., 2011; Stirman et al., 2011; Husson et al., 2012; Kocabas et al., 2012; Fang-Yen et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies using calcium and voltage sensors in C. elegans.

claim: C. elegans neurons and muscles can be manipulated using optogenetics.
source: Worms' optical transparency allows researchers to monitor neural activity with genetically encoded calcium and voltage sensors (Kerr et al., 2000; Kerr, 2006; Flytzanis et al., 2014), and manipulate neurons and muscles using optogenetics (Nagel et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2007; Leifer et al., 2011; Stirman et al., 2011; Husson et al., 2012; Kocabas et al., 2012; Fang-Yen et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to optogenetics studies in C. elegans.

claim: C. elegans is readily amenable to a powerful set of genetic manipulations.
source: C. elegans is readily amenable to a powerful set of genetic manipulations (Ahringer, 2006; Evans, 2006) and shares extensive genetic homology with humans (Lai et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ahringer, 2006 and Evans, 2006.

claim: C. elegans shares extensive genetic homology with humans.
source: C. elegans is readily amenable to a powerful set of genetic manipulations (Ahringer, 2006; Evans, 2006) and shares extensive genetic homology with humans (Lai et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lai et al., 2000.

claim: Classical neurotransmitters involved in C. elegans locomotion include acetylcholine, GABA, glutamate, dopamine, and serotonin.
source: Classical neurotransmitters involved in C. elegans locomotion include acetylcholine (Rand, 2007), GABA (Jorgensen, 2005), glutamate (Brockie and Maricq, 2006), and the biogenic amines dopamine and serotonin (Chase and Koelle, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on neurotransmitters in C. elegans.

claim: C. elegans moves forward by generating sinusoidal dorso-ventral bending waves that propagate from anterior to posterior.
source: C. elegans moves forward by generating sinusoidal dorso-ventral bending waves that propagate from anterior to posterior.
evidence: This is a well-established observation in C. elegans locomotion research and is consistent with general knowledge in the field.

claim: The circuit for C. elegans locomotion consists of interneurons, excitatory and inhibitory motor neurons, and body wall muscles.
source: The circuit for locomotion consists of interneurons, excitatory and inhibitory motor neurons, and body wall muscles (White et al., 1976; Chalfie et al., 1985; White et al., 1986; Altun and Hall, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to foundational studies on C. elegans locomotion circuitry.

claim: The majority of motor neuron cell bodies are located in the ventral nerve cord (VNC) of C. elegans.
source: The majority of motor neuron cell bodies are located in the ventral nerve cord (VNC), which runs along the ventral side of the body from head to tail (White et al., 1986; Altun and Hall, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to White et al., 1986 and Altun and Hall, 2011.

claim: The VNC motor neurons include A, B, VC, D, and AS cell types.
source: The VNC motor neurons include A, B, VC, D, and AS cell types.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans motor neuron classification.

claim: A-type neurons are essential for reverse locomotion in C. elegans.
source: Laser ablation studies have shown that the A-type neurons are essential for reverse locomotion, whereas the B-type are required for forward locomotion (Chalfie et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chalfie et al., 1985, a foundational laser ablation study.

claim: B-type neurons are required for forward locomotion in C. elegans.
source: Laser ablation studies have shown that the A-type neurons are essential for reverse locomotion, whereas the B-type are required for forward locomotion (Chalfie et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chalfie et al., 1985.

claim: D-type (GABAergic) motor neurons are required for a normal amplitude of body bending waves but are not essential for locomotion itself.
source: The D-type (GABAergic) motor neurons are required for a normal amplitude of body bending waves but are not essential for locomotion itself (McIntire et al., 1993b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McIntire et al., 1993b.

claim: The function of the AS neurons is unknown.
source: The function of the AS neurons is unknown.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the text indicating a gap in knowledge.

claim: VC neurons are involved in egg laying in C. elegans.
source: The VC neurons are involved in egg laying (Waggoner et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Waggoner et al., 1998.

claim: All motor neuron classes (A, B, VC, D, AS) form neuromuscular junctions with body wall muscles.
source: These classes all form neuromuscular junctions with body wall muscles (BWMs).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about C. elegans motor neurons.

claim: It is not known which elements generate the worm's dorso-ventral oscillations during forward movement.
source: Perhaps most notably, it is not known which elements generate the worm's dorso-ventral oscillations during forward movement, nor how many such rhythm generators exist.
evidence: This is a direct statement identifying a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: It is unclear how many rhythm generators exist in C. elegans forward locomotion.
source: Perhaps most notably, it is not known which elements generate the worm's dorso-ventral oscillations during forward movement, nor how many such rhythm generators exist.
evidence: This is a direct statement identifying a gap in knowledge.

claim: Worms are capable of limited movement despite ablation of most premotor interneurons.
source: Worms are capable of limited movement despite ablation of most premotor interneurons (Chalfie et al., 1985; Wicks and Rankin, 1995; Zheng et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to ablation studies.

claim: When all premotor interneurons are removed, animals did not generate directional movement, but retained the ability to generate local body bends.
source: When all premotor interneurons are removed, animals did not generate directional movement, but retained the ability to generate local body bends (Kawano et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kawano et al., 2011.

claim: Forward locomotion was observed after ablation of all premotor interneurons and A motor neurons.
source: However, forward locomotion was observed after ablation of all premotor interneurons and A motor neurons (Gao et al, 2017), suggesting that periodic bending during forward locomotion may be organized at the level of the non-A motor neurons and/or the body wall muscles.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gao et al., 2017.

claim: Periodic bending during forward locomotion may be organized at the level of the non-A motor neurons and/or the body wall muscles.
source: However, forward locomotion was observed after ablation of all premotor interneurons and A motor neurons (Gao et al, 2017), suggesting that periodic bending during forward locomotion may be organized at the level of the non-A motor neurons and/or the body wall muscles.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that forward locomotion persists after ablation of premotor interneurons and A motor neurons.

claim: Sensory feedback has been shown to play an important role in coordinating C. elegans motor behavior.
source: Sensory feedback has been shown to play an important role in coordinating C. elegans motor behavior.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent citations and discussion of proprioceptive feedback.

claim: The frequency of C. elegans undulation depends continuously on mechanical loading by its environment.
source: The frequency of C. elegans undulation depends continuously on mechanical loading by its environment (Berri et al., 2009; Fang-Yen et al., 2010), and computational models based on proprioceptive feedback and coupling have recapitulated key aspects of locomotory behavior (Boyle et al., 2012; Wen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berri et al., 2009 and Fang-Yen et al., 2010.

claim: Computational models based on proprioceptive feedback and coupling have recapitulated key aspects of C. elegans locomotory behavior.
source: The frequency of C. elegans undulation depends continuously on mechanical loading by its environment (Berri et al., 2009; Fang-Yen et al., 2010), and computational models based on proprioceptive feedback and coupling have recapitulated key aspects of locomotory behavior (Boyle et al., 2012; Wen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boyle et al., 2012 and Wen et al., 2012.

claim: Experiments in which the worm's body was partially immobilized in a microfluidic device showed that the posterior B-type motor neurons mediate anterior-to-posterior proprioceptive coupling.
source: Experiments in which the worm's body was partially immobilized in a microfluidic device showed that the posterior B-type motor neurons mediate anterior-to-posterior proprioceptive coupling (Wen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wen et al., 2012.

claim: B-type motor neurons sense the body curvature and induce bending in the same direction (ventral or dorsal) posterior to the sensed bending.
source: B-type motor neurons sense the body curvature and induce bending in the same direction (ventral or dorsal) posterior to the sensed bending.
evidence: This is based on the findings from Wen et al., 2012 discussed in the previous sentence.

claim: A model for forward locomotion has been proposed in which a single rhythm generator generates bending undulations in the head, and these undulations propagate through the body from anterior to posterior via proprioceptive coupling.
source: These findings suggested a model for forward locomotion, similar to one proposed earlier (Karbowski et al., 2008), in which a single rhythm generator generates bending undulations in the head, and these undulations propagate through the body from anterior to posterior via proprioceptive coupling (Wen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Karbowski et al., 2008 and Wen et al., 2012.

claim: The single-oscillator model successfully reproduced the continuous variation in locomotory characteristics observed in varied mechanical environments.
source: This model successfully reproduced the continuous variation in locomotory characteristics observed in varied mechanical environments (Berri et al., 2009; Fang-Yen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berri et al., 2009 and Fang-Yen et al., 2010.

claim: The single-oscillator model did not directly address the identity of the rhythmic generator(s).
source: This work, while demonstrating how a wave can be propagated along the body, did not directly address the identity of the rhythmic generator(s).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the limitations of previous work.

claim: The single-oscillator model focused on coupling in the posterior of the worm and did not determine whether head and neck proprioception is similarly essential for bending wave propagation.
source: Furthermore, it focused on coupling in the posterior of the worm and did not determine whether head and neck proprioception is similarly essential for bending wave propagation.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the scope of previous work.

claim: A single-oscillator model with proprioceptive coupling predicts that a disruption in body bending at any location will inhibit posterior bending.
source: A model including a single oscillator with proprioceptive coupling (Figure 1C) predicts that a disruption in body bending at any location will inhibit posterior bending (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the single-oscillator model and illustrated in Figure 1C and 1E.

claim: Alternative models include the presence of multiple oscillators distributed along the motor circuit.
source: Alternative possibilities (Gjorgjieva et al., 2014; Zhen and Samuel, 2015) include the presence of multiple oscillators distributed along the motor circuit (Figure 1D), as in the vertebrate spinal cord (Kiehn, 2006; Mullins et al., 2011; Kiehn, 2016) and in the VNC of some invertebrates (Kristan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gjorgjieva et al., 2014, Zhen and Samuel, 2015, and references to vertebrate and invertebrate models.

claim: Multiple oscillators could be capable of generating undulations in the posterior of the worm even if anterior neural activity or physical bending is interrupted.
source: These oscillatory units could be capable of generating undulations in the posterior of the worm even if anterior neural activity or physical bending is interrupted (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a prediction of the multi-oscillator model illustrated in Figure 1F.

claim: Illuminating body coordinates 50–65 in Pmyo-3::NpHR worms caused substantial paralysis in the tail.
source: Illuminating body coordinates 50–65 in Pmyo-3::NpHR worms caused substantial paralysis in the tail (not shown), consistent with previous findings (Leifer et al., 2011; Wen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Leifer et al., 2011 and Wen et al., 2012.

claim: When the anterior 33% or 45% of the worm was paralyzed, robust oscillations were observed in posterior regions of the body.
source: When we paralyzed the anterior 33% or 45% of the worm, however, we observed robust oscillations in posterior regions of the body.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments described.

claim: Illumination of the anterior 33% of the body caused the tail's undulation frequency to increase.
source: In addition, we found to our surprise that illumination of the anterior 33% of the body caused the tail's undulation frequency to increase (Figure 2A,D; Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and 2D.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of cholinergic neurons in the head and neck caused anterior paralysis, but tail undulation often persisted.
source: We found that while optogenetic inhibition of cholinergic neurons in the head and neck caused anterior paralysis, tail undulation often persisted (Figure 2B,D, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and 2D.

claim: During optogenetic muscle or neuron inactivation, the amplitude of the bending wave in the head decreased greatly but did not vanish.
source: During optogenetic muscle or neuron inactivation, the amplitude of the bending wave in the head decreased greatly but did not vanish (Figure 2A,B,E), leaving open the possibility that a residual small amplitude wave allows propagation of the bending wave through the partially paralyzed region.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A, 2B, and 2E.

claim: Region-targeted illumination at 470 nm of Pmyo-3::PH::miniSOG worms selectively lesioned muscles.
source: To selectively lesion muscles, we used region-targeted illumination at 470 nm of Pmyo-3::PH::miniSOG worms in which the photosensitizing protein miniSOG is expressed in body wall muscles (Xu and Chisholm, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu and Chisholm, 2016 and the experimental description.

claim: The anterior portion of most miniSOG-treated animals was nearly immobile, yet undulation posterior to the region of illumination was routinely observed.
source: The anterior portion of most treated animals was nearly immobile (Figure 2C, Video 1, especially the last 8 s). Nevertheless, undulation posterior to the region of illumination was routinely observed in these animals.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and Video 1.

claim: After thermal lesioning of the anterior half of the worm with a hot platinum wire, the animal's head and neck were nearly motionless, yet rhythmic undulation routinely persisted in the tail.
source: We also conducted thermal lesioning experiments in which touched the anterior half of the worm with a hot platinum wire attached to a soldering iron. After this treatment, the animal's head and neck were again nearly motionless, yet rhythmic undulation routinely persisted in the tail (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Video 1.

claim: The finding that posterior undulation can persist despite anterior paralysis is consistent with a multi-oscillator model and not with a single oscillator model that relies on reflex-like signaling for wave propagation.
source: Our finding that posterior undulation can persist despite anterior paralysis is consistent with a multi-oscillator model (Figure 1D) and not with a single oscillator model that relies on reflex-like signaling for wave propagation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results in relation to the two models presented in Figure 1.

claim: Optogenetically inhibiting neck muscles prevented waves generated in the head from propagating through the neck in most trials.
source: In most trials, optogenetically inhibiting neck muscles prevented waves generated in the head from propagating through the neck.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments.

claim: During the interruption of head waves by neck muscle inhibition, the tail exhibited bending undulations at a higher frequency than that of the head, resulting in two-frequency undulation (2FU).
source: During the interruption of these waves, the tail exhibited bending undulations at a higher frequency than that of the head, resulting in the animal simultaneously undulating at two distinct frequencies (Figure 3A, Video 2). We henceforth refer to this behavior, whether or not induced by any manipulation, as two-frequency undulation (2FU).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Video 2.

claim: 2FU was observed upon inhibiting all neck cholinergic neurons.
source: We observed 2FU upon inhibiting all neck cholinergic neurons (Figure 3B, Video 2) and also upon inhibiting neck B-type motor neurons (Pacr-5::Arch; Figure 3C, Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and Video 2.

claim: 2FU was observed upon inhibiting neck B-type motor neurons.
source: We observed 2FU upon inhibiting all neck cholinergic neurons (Figure 3B, Video 2) and also upon inhibiting neck B-type motor neurons (Pacr-5::Arch; Figure 3C, Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C and Video 2.

claim: These manipulations led to a large decrease in wave amplitude in the neck and a smaller decrease in wave amplitude in the tail.
source: These manipulations led to a large decrease in wave amplitude in the neck and a smaller decrease in wave amplitude in the tail (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Multiple animals in each experiment showed 2FU, with the highest ratios of tail frequency to head frequency seen in worms in which the neck muscles were inhibited.
source: Nevertheless, multiple animals in each experiment showed 2FU, with the highest ratios of tail frequency to head frequency seen in worms in which the neck muscles were inhibited (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The bending amplitude of the tail generally decreased as the frequency increased.
source: The bending amplitude of the tail generally decreased as the frequency increased (Figure 3E,F), consistent with the changes in bending frequency and amplitude previously observed when the viscosity of a fluid environment was varied (Fang-Yen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E and 3F, and is consistent with previous findings cited.

claim: The opposite trends of amplitude and frequency may reflect a constraint to the maximum absolute rate of change of curvature, which is proportional to the product of amplitude and frequency.
source: The opposite trends of amplitude and frequency may reflect a constraint to the maximum absolute rate of change of curvature, which is proportional to the product of amplitude and frequency.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed relationship between amplitude and frequency.

claim: Lesioning mid-body muscles in Pmyo-3::PH::miniSOG worms led to stronger decoupling between head and tail oscillations, but did not prevent 2FU.
source: To test whether 2FU can occur after stronger disruption of motor coupling, we lesioned mid-body muscles in Pmyo-3::PH::miniSOG worms. This manipulation indeed led to stronger decoupling between head and tail oscillations, but did still not prevent 2FU (Figure 3D, Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D and Video 2.

claim: Selective activation of small portions of the tail motor circuit while inhibiting the rest led to high-frequency localized undulations in the tail in several animals.
source: We therefore examined worms in which both the inhibitory opsin NpHR and the excitatory opsin Channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) were expressed in the cholinergic neurons, after the A-type motor neurons were ablated by Punc-4::miniSOG. We first illuminated these animals with 590 nm wavelength (yellow) light throughout the body to inhibit all cholinergic neurons. While maintaining this yellow illumination, we targeted small portions of the tail with 473 nm wavelength (blue) light, activating ChR2 and stimulating a few posterior B and AS neurons. Under these conditions, several animals generated high-frequency localized undulations in the tail (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and Video 3.

claim: Independent head and tail oscillations were observed in animals without induced lesions or optogenetic perturbations when transitioning between regions of different viscosities.
source: When we studied worms transitioning between regions of a low-viscosity buffer into highly viscoelastic hydroxypropylmethylcellulose (HPMC) islands (see Methods), we observed 2FU in 6 of 41 worms (15%). In these animals, the tail continued oscillating at a high frequency for at least two full cycles even as the head frequency was sharply reduced (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and Video 3.

claim: 2FU can occur in C. elegans with no internal perturbations.
source: Although these events were uncommon, they demonstrated that 2FU can occur in C. elegans with no internal perturbations.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of 2FU in worms transitioning between different viscosity environments.

claim: The C. elegans forward motor circuit contains at least two units capable of independent rhythm generation.
source: Taken together, these results strongly suggest that the C. elegans forward motor circuit contains at least two units capable of independent rhythm generation and that a partial breakdown in anterior proprioceptive coupling (for example by inhibiting neck BWMs) is sufficient to reveal the presence of the posterior oscillating unit(s).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the multiple experiments showing 2FU under various conditions.

claim: A partial breakdown in anterior proprioceptive coupling is sufficient to reveal the presence of posterior oscillating unit(s).
source: Taken together, these results strongly suggest that the C. elegans forward motor circuit contains at least two units capable of independent rhythm generation and that a partial breakdown in anterior proprioceptive coupling (for example by inhibiting neck BWMs) is sufficient to reveal the presence of the posterior oscillating unit(s).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing 2FU upon disruption of coupling.

claim: Almost all chemical or electrical synaptic connections to the VNC motor neurons are made by the premotor interneuron classes AVB, PVC, AVA, AVD, and AVE.
source: Almost all chemical or electrical synaptic connections to the VNC motor neurons are made by the premotor interneuron (IN) classes AVB, PVC, AVA, AVD, and AVE (White et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citation to White et al., 1986.

claim: Laser ablation studies have indicated that AVB, and to a lesser degree PVC, are essential for normal forward locomotion.
source: Laser ablation studies have indicated that AVB, and to a lesser degree PVC, are essential for normal forward locomotion (Chalfie et al., 1985), although rudimentary forward crawling is possible in their absence if the reverse-driving A motor neurons are also removed (Gao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chalfie et al., 1985 and Gao et al., 2017.

claim: Rudimentary forward crawling is possible in the absence of AVB and PVC if the reverse-driving A motor neurons are also removed.
source: Laser ablation studies have indicated that AVB, and to a lesser degree PVC, are essential for normal forward locomotion (Chalfie et al., 1985), although rudimentary forward crawling is possible in their absence if the reverse-driving A motor neurons are also removed (Gao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gao et al., 2017.

claim: Both Pnmr-1::ICE and Pglr-1::ICE strains were capable of 2FU during optogenetic inhibition of neck muscles.
source: We found that both strains were capable of 2FU during optogenetic inhibition of neck muscles (Figure 4A,E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A, 4E, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, 1E.

claim: 2FU does not require most premotor interneurons, including the forward locomotory interneurons PVC.
source: This result demonstrates that 2FU does not require most premotor interneurons, including the forward locomotory interneurons neurons PVC.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that 2FU occurs in Pnmr-1::ICE and Pglr-1::ICE strains.

claim: unc-7 and unc-9 worms were capable of 2FU.
source: We found that both strains were capable of 2FU, although it appeared to occur less often than in PVC-ablated animals, and sometimes occurred prior to neck muscle inhibition (Figure 4B,E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E; Figure 4—figure supplement 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B, 4E, and supplementary figures.

claim: The UNC-7/UNC-9 gap junctions, including those between AVB and the B-type motor neurons, are not required for 2FU.
source: This finding shows that the UNC-7/UNC-9 gap junctions, including those between AVB and the B-type motor neurons, are not required for 2FU.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that unc-7 and unc-9 mutants can exhibit 2FU.

claim: After ablation of AVB, 2FU events were nearly diminished.
source: When subjected to the same experiment as described above, 2FU events were nearly diminished. Very rarely we observed uncoupled undulation events that were not correlated with neck muscle inhibition (Figure 4—figure supplements 1B, E, 2 and 5C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 1B, 1E, 2, and 5C.

claim: Most individual classes of premotor interneurons, including AVA, AVD, AVE, and PVC, are not essential for 2FU.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that most individual classes of premotor interneurons, including AVA, AVD, AVE, and PVC, are not essential for 2FU. However, AVB may play a key role in activating the rhythm generator(s) to allow oscillation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the various ablation experiments.

claim: AVB may play a key role in activating the rhythm generator(s) to allow oscillation.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that most individual classes of premotor interneurons, including AVA, AVD, AVE, and PVC, are not essential for 2FU. However, AVB may play a key role in activating the rhythm generator(s) to allow oscillation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that AVB ablation nearly eliminates 2FU.

claim: Ablating the A- and VC-type motor neurons with Punc-4::miniSOG did not prevent 2FU induced by neck paralysis during forward locomotion.
source: We found that ablating the A- and VC-type motor neurons with a genetically targeted ROS generator (Punc-4::miniSOG) did not prevent 2FU induced by neck paralysis during forward locomotion (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and 1E.

claim: The A and VC motor neurons are not necessary for the posterior forward oscillator(s).
source: This result supports the idea that the A and VC motor neurons are not necessary for the posterior forward oscillator(s).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that 2FU occurs without A and VC motor neurons.

claim: Animals harboring an unc-49(e407) mutation were capable of 2FU during neck muscle paralysis.
source: We found that animals harboring an unc-49(e407) mutation, while very slow swimmers, were nonetheless capable of 2FU during neck muscle paralysis (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: 2FU occurred very rarely after ablating DB3, VB3, and VB4 or VB8 and VB9.
source: 2FU was observed very rarely after ablating DB3, VB3, and VB4 or VB8 and VB9 (Figure 4C,F), although in both conditions there were additional instances of 2FU that occurred outside the time 3 s window used for frequency analysis (Fouad et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C and 4F.

claim: 2FU occurred repeatedly, although not commonly, in all other B motor neuron ablation conditions tested.
source: 2FU occurred repeatedly, although not commonly, in all other conditions. (Figure 4F; Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4F and supplementary figures.

claim: In the presence of premotor interneurons, the B class motor neurons contribute to neck-paralysis induced 2FU, but no single member is essential for generating high-frequency tail rhythms during 2FU.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that in the presence of premotor interneurons, the B class motor neurons contribute to neck-paralysis induced 2FU, but no single member is essential for generating high-frequency tail rhythms during 2FU.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the various B motor neuron ablation experiments.

claim: The A, VC and D motor neurons are not required for 2FU.
source: The A, VC and D motor neurons are not required for 2FU.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ablation experiments.

claim: Posterior rhythm generation can arise from multiple subsets of B or AS motor neurons.
source: Our results are consistent with a model in which posterior rhythm generation can arise from multiple subsets of B or AS motor neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative model consistent with the experimental results.

claim: vab-7 mutants had mildly or strongly paralyzed tails and were incapable of 2FU when neck muscles were inhibited.
source: We found that vab-7 mutants had mildly or strongly paralyzed tails and were incapable of 2FU when neck muscles were inhibited, suggesting that vab-7 is essential for 2FU (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and 1E.

claim: vab-7 is essential for 2FU.
source: We found that vab-7 mutants had mildly or strongly paralyzed tails and were incapable of 2FU when neck muscles were inhibited, suggesting that vab-7 is essential for 2FU (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that vab-7 mutants cannot perform 2FU.

claim: Worms in which most DB motor neurons were eliminated were dramatically less likely to show 2FU than mock controls, but were not incapable of doing so.
source: Worms in which most DB motor neurons were eliminated were dramatically less likely to show 2FU than mock controls, but were not incapable of doing so (Figure 5, Video 4; N = 9 out of 104 trials from 25 worms by blinded, randomized scoring).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5 and Video 4.

claim: Elimination of most VB motor neurons sharply reduced but did not eliminate the incidence of 2FU.
source: We performed the converse experiment – elimination of most VB motor neurons using our infrared laser system – and found the incidence of 2FU was again sharply reduced but not eliminated (Figure 5, Video 4, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5, Video 4, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: When both DB and most VB motor neurons were removed, animals were incapable of 2FU.
source: When we combined miniSOG and laser ablation to remove all DB and most VB motor neurons, animals were incapable of 2FU (Figure 5; 0 out of 102 trials from 27 worms by blinded, randomized scoring).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The B motor neurons as a class are essential for independent tail undulation during forward movement.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the B motor neurons as a class are essential for independent tail undulation during forward movement.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that removal of both DB and VB eliminates 2FU.

claim: The B motor neurons have a role in generating the high-frequency locomotory rhythm observed in 2FU.
source: Our results are consistent with the hypothesis that the B motor neurons have a role in generating the high-frequency locomotory rhythm observed in 2FU.
evidence: This is a hypothesis consistent with the experimental results.

claim: Severing both the VNC and the dorsal nerve cord (DNC) just posterior to the pharynx eliminated synaptic connections between the mid-body motor neurons and the head circuits.
source: To ascertain whether the mid-body motor circuit is capable of independent rhythm generation, we developed a method for eliminating synaptic connections between the mid-body motor neurons and the head circuits. We used our infrared laser system to sever both the VNC and the dorsal nerve cord (DNC) just posterior to the pharynx.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used.

claim: In many cases, severing the VNC and DNC also severed other fasciculated process bundles that run parallel to the VNC and DNC.
source: In many cases, this procedure also severed other fasciculated process bundles that run parallel to the VNC and DNC (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Most animals were inactive several hours after disruption of the nerve cords, but active forward locomotion was induced by application of a mechanical stimulus.
source: Several hours after disruption of the nerve cords, most animals were inactive (data not shown), but active forward locomotion was induced by application of a mechanical stimulus.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments.

claim: Most worms with severed VNC and DNC could generate robust oscillations posterior to the cut location.
source: Most of these worms could generate robust oscillations posterior to the cut location (Figure 6A,E, Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A, 6E, and Video 5.

claim: The tail often undulated at a higher frequency than the mid-body in worms with severed VNC and DNC.
source: Moreover, the tail often undulated at a higher frequency than the mid-body (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: In some cases, low-amplitude waves propagating in the posterior-to-anterior direction occurred simultaneously with robust mid-body and tail waves propagating in the anterior-to-posterior direction.
source: In some cases, low-amplitude waves propagating in the posterior-to-anterior direction occurred simultaneously with robust mid-body and tail waves propagating in the anterior-to-posterior direction (Figure 6A, Video 5), suggesting a deficit in coordination between circuits on either side of the lesion.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A and Video 5.

claim: Synaptic connections from the head circuits to the motor neurons may not be essential for wave generation posterior to the head.
source: These results suggest that synaptic connections from the head circuits to the motor neurons may not be essential for wave generation posterior to the head.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that oscillations occur posterior to VNC/DNC cuts.

claim: VNC-lesioned worms exhibited very little movement in the head but continued to generate robust oscillations in the mid-body and even higher frequency oscillations in the tail.
source: Animals treated with these three lesions are henceforth referred to as 'VNC-lesioned' worms. These worms exhibited very little movement in the head. However, they continued to generate robust oscillations in the mid-body and even higher frequency oscillations in the tail (Figure 6B,E, Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6B, 6E, and Video 5.

claim: The pattern of locomotion in VNC-lesioned animals strongly resembled the 2FU induced by optogenetic perturbation, with the important difference that in the lesioned preparation, both frequencies were likely generated outside the head.
source: The pattern of locomotion in VNC-lesioned animals strongly resembled the 2FU induced by optogenetic perturbation, with the important difference that in our lesioned preparation, both frequencies were likely generated outside the head.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the VNC-lesioned results to the optogenetic 2FU results.

claim: The VNC motor circuit itself may contain multiple units capable of independent oscillation.
source: The emergence of multiple frequencies of undulation outside the head suggests that the VNC motor circuit itself may contain multiple units capable of independent oscillation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of multiple frequencies in VNC-lesioned worms.

claim: When the VNC and DNC were cut in two locations (in the neck and in the tail), animals could generate robust body oscillations posterior to the first cut and higher frequency oscillations posterior to the second cut.
source: To test this possibility directly, we cut the VNC and DNC in two locations: in the neck (anterior to VB3) and in the tail (posterior to VB8). We again thermally lesioned the head neurons to suppress head movement. Under these conditions, the VNC motor neurons between VB3 and VB8 are isolated from circuitry in both the head and tail, and the VNC motor neurons posterior to VB8 are isolated from both the head circuits and the anterior VNC motor neurons. As before, these animals could generate robust body oscillations posterior to the first cut and higher frequency oscillations posterior to the second cut (Figure 6C,E, Video 5), suggesting that rhythms can arise independently from each of these portions of the VNC motor neurons.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C, 6E, and Video 5.

claim: Rhythms can arise independently from multiple portions of the VNC motor neurons.
source: As before, these animals could generate robust body oscillations posterior to the first cut and higher frequency oscillations posterior to the second cut (Figure 6C,E, Video 5), suggesting that rhythms can arise independently from each of these portions of the VNC motor neurons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the double VNC/DNC cut experiments.

claim: The A motor neurons are not required for body oscillation in VNC-lesioned worms.
source: We severed the VNC and DNC in either one or two locations after ablating the A motor neurons with Punc-4::miniSOG. Animals in which the VNC and DNC had been severed near the head were capable of robust wave generation and propagation posterior to the head (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B). Animals in which the VNC and DNC were severed in two locations were capable of rhythmic activity in the mid-body or tail, although we did not observe any cases of simultaneous oscillation in each segment (N = 20 worms, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C). These results support the idea that the A motor neurons are not required for generation of rhythmic forward waves in surgically isolated segments of the VNC motor circuit.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and 1C.

claim: The B motor neurons are required for rhythm generation in VNC-lesioned worms.
source: To test this idea, we used VNC-lesioned worms in which the DA and DB motor neurons were ablated by miniSOG and the VB motor neurons were ablated by an infrared laser as before. After nerve cord surgery, worms in either B-ablation condition, like mock controls, were highly inactive. Application of a mechanical stimulus caused tight coiling, especially but not exclusively in the DB-only ablation condition (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C, Video 6). Despite this coiling, we observed at least one case of a VNC-lesioned, DB-ablated worm appearing to move the very tip of its tail, possibly in a rhythmic fashion, suggesting that DB neurons may not be required for rudimentary oscillation in at least the most posterior portion of the tail. However, in VNC-isolated worms for which most DB and VB neurons were ablated, we never observed rhythmic movements (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D–F; N = 19 mechanical stimulus trials from nine worms). These results suggest that, as was the case for optogenetic 2FU, the B motor neurons are required for rhythm generation in VNC-lesioned worms.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C-F and Video 6.

claim: Anterior VNC/DNC cuts disrupt normal head undulation.
source: The observation that anterior VNC/DNC cuts disrupt normal head undulation (Figure 6A) suggests that rhythm generation by the head circuit may require inputs from the VNC.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Rhythm generation by the head circuit may require inputs from the VNC.
source: The observation that anterior VNC/DNC cuts disrupt normal head undulation (Figure 6A) suggests that rhythm generation by the head circuit may require inputs from the VNC.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that head undulation is disrupted after VNC/DNC cuts.

claim: Very slow head undulation was occasionally observed in animals with VNC/DNC cuts in two locations slightly more posterior to the head, indicating that head undulation is still possible under these conditions.
source: However, we occasionally observed very slow head undulation in these animals, indicating that head undulation is still possible under these conditions (Figure 6D, Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6D and Video 5.

claim: Input from the posterior motor circuit may be essential for the normal frequency of head undulation.
source: Another possibility is that input from the posterior motor circuit is essential for the normal frequency of head undulation. The latter hypothesis may be supported by our earlier observation that strong decoupling of head and tail oscillations by muscle ablation (i.e. without lesioning the nerve cord or parallel tracts) resulted in similarly slow head oscillations (Figure 3D), while weak decoupling resulted in moderately slower head oscillations (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by observations from Figures 3A and 3D.

claim: The C. elegans forward locomotor circuitry possesses at least three units capable of independent oscillation, with two units located outside the head.
source: These results suggest that the C. elegans forward locomotor circuitry possesses at least three units capable of independent oscillation, with two units located outside the head.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the VNC/DNC lesioning experiments.

claim: Oscillations are possible in each segment when isolated from the others.
source: Although we did not observe simultaneous three-frequency forward undulation in any animal tested, we have shown that oscillations are possible in each segment when isolated from the others.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: When the VNC and DNC were severed at any one of a number of different locations, undulations posterior to the damage arose near each cut location.
source: When we severed the VNC and DNC at any one of a number of different locations (anterior to VB3, VB5, VB6, VB7, VB9, VB10, and VB11), we found that undulations posterior to the damage arose near each cut location (Figure 7B–E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B-E.

claim: Bending amplitude recovered just posterior to each cut location, rather than at a fixed body coordinate.
source: Bending amplitude similarly recovered just posterior to each cut location, rather than at a fixed body coordinate (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Oscillations in the tail usually had a higher frequency when the nerve cords were severed in the tail than when they were severed near the head.
source: Oscillations in the tail usually had a higher frequency when the nerve cords were severed in the tail than when they were severed near the head (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: The smallest VNC segment that produced clear and robust rhythmic waves was the region between VB9 and the tail.
source: The smallest VNC segment that produced clear and robust rhythmic waves was the region between VB9 and the tail.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the systematic VNC/DNC severing experiments.

claim: The most compact rhythm-generating unit of the forward motor circuit is at least as small as the region containing VB9, VB10, VB11, DB6, and DB7.
source: These results suggest that the most compact rhythm-generating unit of the forward motor circuit is at least as small as the region containing VB9, VB10, VB11, DB6, and DB7.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that this region can generate rhythms when isolated.

claim: During 2FU, head frequency decreases relative to the unperturbed swimming frequency.
source: We found that during 2FU, head frequency decreases relative to the unperturbed swimming frequency (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Slowing of head frequency was often even more dramatic when decoupling was stronger.
source: Slowing was often even more dramatic when decoupling was stronger (Figures 3D and 6D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 3D and 6D.

claim: Anteriorward coupling, in addition to posteriorward coupling, may be present in the forward locomotor circuitry.
source: These observations suggest that anteriorward coupling, in addition to posteriorward coupling, may be present in the forward locomotor circuitry.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that head frequency decreases during 2FU.

claim: Rhythmically inhibiting the mid-body BWMs caused worms to exhibit a head bending frequency approximately one half that of the imposed frequency.
source: Worms subjected to this procedure exhibited a head bending frequency approximately one half that of the imposed frequency.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the rhythmic optogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: The factor of one half in the entrainment is likely due to the presence of two phases during the rhythmic locomotory cycle of any single part of the body during which the curvature is close to zero (i.e. muscles are relaxed).
source: The factor of one half is likely due to the presence of two phases during the rhythmic locomotory cycle of any single part of the body during which the curvature is close to zero (i.e. muscles are relaxed).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed 1:2 entrainment ratio.

claim: The head frequency could be entrained to a range of imposed mid-body frequencies.
source: We found the head frequency could be entrained to a range of imposed mid-body frequencies. Subjecting body coordinates 33–66 to pulsed illumination at frequencies from approximately 1 to 2 Hz caused an increase in the power spectrum of the worm's oscillations at frequencies corresponding to half of the imposed frequency, and a decrease at other frequencies. Pulsing at frequencies below 1 Hz generally led to head oscillations near the imposed frequency (Figure 8C(ii)).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8C(ii).

claim: A mid-body rhythmic signal can entrain head bending.
source: These results show that a mid-body rhythmic signal can entrain head bending, and point to the presence of an anteriorward coupling mechanism within the motor circuit.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rhythmic optogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: There is an anteriorward coupling mechanism within the motor circuit.
source: These results show that a mid-body rhythmic signal can entrain head bending, and point to the presence of an anteriorward coupling mechanism within the motor circuit.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the entrainment experiments.

claim: Rhythmic optogenetic inhibition of the midbody cholinergic neurons caused worms to adjust their head bending frequency to match one-half of the imposed frequency.
source: We applied a rhythmic optogenetic inhibition pattern to the midbody cholinergic neurons in Punc-17::NpHR worms. Once again, worms subject to this procedure quickly adjust their head bending frequency to match one-half of the imposed frequency (Figure 8D(i), Video 7).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8D(i) and Video 7.

claim: Rhythmic illumination of the tail cholinergic neurons at 2 Hz increased the magnitude of head bending at 1 Hz.
source: Moreover, rhythmic illumination of the tail cholinergic neurons at 2 Hz similarly increased the magnitude of head bending at 1 Hz (Figure 8D(ii)).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8D(ii).

claim: Selective rhythmic hyperpolarization of the mid-body B motor neurons sufficed to increase the magnitude of head bending at one-half of the stimulus frequency.
source: Selective rhythmic hyperpolarization of the mid-body B motor neurons also sufficed to increase the magnitude of head bending at one-half of the stimulus frequency (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), as did rhythmic hyperpolarization of the BWMs when muscle-to-muscle gap junctions were disrupted in only in the BWMs by a mutation in the innexin unc-9 that was rescued in neurons but not muscles (Wen et al., 2012) (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claim: The posterior to anterior coupling is mediated neuronally, possibly by the VNC motor neurons.
source: These observations suggest that the posterior to anterior coupling is mediated neuronally, possibly by the VNC motor neurons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the various rhythmic inhibition experiments.

claim: In zebrafish and lampreys, rhythmogenic capability for swimming undulations is distributed along the rostro-caudal axis of the spinal cord.
source: In zebrafish and lampreys, rhythmogenic capability for swimming undulations is distributed along the rostro-caudal axis of the spinal cord (Kiehn, 2006; Mullins et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kiehn, 2006 and Mullins et al., 2011.

claim: When isolated from the rest of the cord, groups of lamprey spinal segments do not exhibit identical preferred frequencies.
source: When isolated from the rest of the cord, groups of lamprey spinal segments do not exhibit identical preferred frequencies (Cohen, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cohen, 1987.

claim: In the swimming intact lamprey, oscillations in all segments are phase and frequency-locked by intersegmental coupling that spans broad swaths of the spine.
source: In the swimming intact animal, oscillations in all segments are phase and frequency-locked by intersegmental coupling that spans broad swaths of the spine (Mullins et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mullins et al., 2011.

claim: The motor system of the leech also shows a distributed rhythm generating architecture.
source: The motor system of the leech, an invertebrate, also shows a distributed rhythm generating architecture.
evidence: This is established knowledge about leech motor systems.

claim: Individual ganglia of the leech VNC can generate crude bursting patterns that resemble their firing patterns during swimming.
source: Individual ganglia of the leech VNC can generate crude bursting patterns that resemble their firing patterns during swimming.
evidence: This is established knowledge about leech motor systems.

claim: The most robustly oscillating ganglia in the leech are towards the middle of the leech's body.
source: The most robustly oscillating ganglia are towards the middle of the leech's body, and isolated midbody ganglia also have a higher frequency than isolated ganglia near either the head or tail.
evidence: This is established knowledge about leech motor systems.

claim: Isolated midbody ganglia in the leech have a higher frequency than isolated ganglia near either the head or tail.
source: The most robustly oscillating ganglia are towards the middle of the leech's body, and isolated midbody ganglia also have a higher frequency than isolated ganglia near either the head or tail.
evidence: This is established knowledge about leech motor systems.

claim: In the intact leech, extensive, bidirectional intersegmental coupling drives the system to adopt a single locomotor frequency.
source: In the intact animal, extensive, bidirectional intersegmental coupling drives the system to adopt a single locomotor frequency (Pearce and Friesen, 1985; Kristan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pearce and Friesen, 1985 and Kristan et al., 2005.

claim: The results reveal a picture of forward locomotor control in C. elegans similar to that found in the lamprey and leech.
source: Our results reveal a picture of forward locomotor control in C. elegans similar to that found in the lamprey and leech.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the C. elegans results to those from other organisms.

claim: Rhythmogenic capability in the worm is distributed along the VNC motor circuit.
source: We found that rhythmogenic capability in the worm is distributed along the VNC motor circuit.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: As in other swimming models, the rhythm-generating capability of posterior circuits is only detectable when coupling is disrupted.
source: As in other swimming models, the rhythm-generating capability of posterior circuits is only detectable when coupling is disrupted.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results and comparison to other models.

claim: The incomplete nature of the optogenetic decoupling method yielded evidence that an anterior rhythm can entrain the higher frequency posterior rhythms.
source: The incomplete nature of our optogenetic decoupling method yielded evidence that an anterior rhythm can entrain the higher frequency posterior rhythms. For example, we found that during 2FU, some but not all waves in the tail were continuous with waves in the head (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from observations in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Neither the head nor tail frequency during 2FU matched the natural (unperturbed) frequency of locomotion.
source: We found that neither the head nor tail frequency during 2FU matched the natural (unperturbed) frequency of locomotion.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments.

claim: The normal locomotory frequency in the environment of the assay was generally intermediate between the head and tail frequencies exhibited during 2FU.
source: Instead, the normal locomotory frequency in the environment of the assay was generally intermediate between the head and tail frequencies exhibited during 2FU.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments.

claim: During locomotion, multiple rhythm generating units, each with different rhythmic properties, are combined by strong inter-unit coupling to form one functional unit.
source: This finding shows another key similarity with models of swimming in other vertebrates and invertebrates: during locomotion, multiple rhythm generating units, each with different rhythmic properties, are combined by strong inter-unit coupling to form one functional unit (Friesen and Hocker, 2001; Kristan et al., 2005; Kiehn, 2006; Mullins et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on other organisms and is consistent with the C. elegans findings.

claim: A whole-body oscillating unit will generally have rhythmic properties different from that of any subunit in isolation.
source: Such a whole-body oscillating unit will generally have rhythmic properties different from that of any subunit in isolation.
evidence: This is a general principle inferred from the experimental results and comparison to other systems.

claim: Modeling studies of the leech swim CPG have suggested that the overall fictive locomotor frequency of a 17-ganglion portion of the VNC lies within the range of frequencies of the individual ganglia.
source: Indeed, modeling studies of the leech swim CPG have suggested that the overall fictive locomotor frequency of a 17-ganglion portion of the VNC lies within the range of frequencies of the individual ganglia (Zheng et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zheng et al., 2007.

claim: The gradient in intrinsic frequencies appears to set the wavelength during fictive swimming in the leech.
source: The gradient in intrinsic frequencies appears to set the wavelength during fictive swimming.
evidence: This is a statement about leech swimming based on modeling studies.

claim: The variation in rhythmic properties between different parts of the body may play a similar role in C. elegans.
source: The variation in rhythmic properties between different parts of the body may play a similar role in C. elegans.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis drawn from comparison to the leech.

claim: During forward locomotion, the C. elegans motor circuit is coupled by posteriorward proprioception and additional anteriorward and posteriorward coupling mechanisms.
source: During forward locomotion, the C. elegans motor circuit is coupled by posteriorward proprioception (Wen et al., 2012), and additional anteriorward and posteriorward coupling mechanisms (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wen et al., 2012 and the experimental results shown in Figure 8.

claim: Bidirectional coupling appears to allow the entire C. elegans motor circuit to operate as one unit.
source: This bidirectional coupling appears to allow the entire circuit to operate as one unit.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: This picture is similar to descriptions of leech and lamprey motor circuits.
source: This picture is similar to descriptions of leech and lamprey motor circuits.
evidence: This is a comparison drawn between C. elegans and other organisms.

claim: In the leech, oscillatory interneurons that comprise the swim CPG send axons along the anterior-posterior axis of the animal, and mediate bidirectional coupling between midbody ganglia.
source: In the leech, oscillatory interneurons that comprise the swim CPG send axons along the anterior-posterior axis of the animal, and mediate bidirectional coupling between midbody ganglia (Friesen and Hocker, 2001; Kristan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Friesen and Hocker, 2001 and Kristan et al., 2005.

claim: The coupling between ganglia in the leech appears to result from a mixture of proprioceptive feedback and central control.
source: The coupling between ganglia appears to result from a mixture of proprioceptive feedback and central control (Yu et al., 1999; Kristan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yu et al., 1999 and Kristan et al., 2005.

claim: Injection of sinusoidally varying current into the leech stretch receptor cells was sufficient to entrain swimming activity at the injection frequency.
source: Injection of sinusoidally varying current into the leech stretch receptor cells was sufficient to entrain swimming activity (Yu and Friesen, 2004) at the injection frequency.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yu and Friesen, 2004.

claim: Imposed rhythmic movements are capable of entraining fictive swimming in isolated preparations of the lamprey spinal cord.
source: Imposed rhythmic movements are also capable of entraining fictive swimming in isolated preparations of the lamprey spinal cord (Grillner et al., 1981; McClellan and Sigvardt, 1988) and several other vertebrate and invertebrate systems (Wendler, 1974; Andersson et al., 1981; Robertson and Pearson, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on various organisms.

claim: The results include several lines of evidence implicating the cholinergic B and AS motor neurons as a likely source of posterior rhythmogenesis during C. elegans forward locomotion.
source: Our results include several lines of evidence implicating the cholinergic B and AS motor neurons as a likely source of posterior rhythmogenesis during C. elegans forward locomotion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results.

claim: Disruption or removal of most or all B motor neurons virtually abolished independent tail undulations induced either optogenetically or by severing the nerve cords.
source: First, disruption or removal of most or all B motor neurons virtually abolished independent tail undulations induced either optogenetically or by severing the nerve cords, but elimination of other motor neurons and premotor interneurons did not eliminate the ability of the posterior to oscillate independently (Figures 4, 5 and 6).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 4, 5, and 6.

claim: Stimulation of select B and AS neurons after paralyzing most of the body led to local, high-frequency oscillations in the tail that mimicked 2FU.
source: Second, stimulation of select B and AS neurons after paralyzing most of the body led to local, high-frequency oscillations in the tail that mimicked 2FU (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Imposing a rhythmic signal on mid-body B motor neurons sufficed to entrain whole-body locomotor frequency.
source: Third, imposing a rhythmic signal on mid-body B motor neurons sufficed to entrain whole-body locomotor frequency, as did imposing rhythms on the broader class of cholinergic neurons and the body wall muscles (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Changes in body posture are sensed by the B motor neurons, providing a likely explanation for how the BWM manipulation was able to entrain locomotion.
source: Changes in body posture are sensed by the B motor neurons (Wen et al., 2012), providing a likely explanation for how the BWM manipulation was able to entrain locomotion.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wen et al., 2012 and provides an explanation for the experimental results.

claim: The swimming frequency, and thus phase, was reset almost immediately after the first inhibitory stimulus in the rhythmic optogenetic experiments.
source: In our experiments, the swimming frequency, and thus phase, was reset almost immediately after the first inhibitory stimulus, suggesting that the B motor neurons share the phase shifting property with oscillatory interneurons in the leech.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the rhythmic optogenetic experiments.

claim: The B motor neurons share the phase shifting property with oscillatory interneurons in the leech.
source: In our experiments, the swimming frequency, and thus phase, was reset almost immediately after the first inhibitory stimulus, suggesting that the B motor neurons share the phase shifting property with oscillatory interneurons in the leech.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of phase resetting and comparison to leech interneurons.

claim: The B motor neurons are rhythmically active in phase with locomotion.
source: Lastly, the B motor neurons are rhythmically active in phase with locomotion (Kawano et al., 2011; Wen et al., 2012), satisfying another key criterion set for candidate oscillator neurons in the leech (Mullins et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kawano et al., 2011 and Wen et al., 2012.

claim: Descriptions of swimming CPGs in vertebrates have tended to exclude motor neurons as members of the CPG, with most oscillatory function attributed to interneurons.
source: Descriptions of swimming CPGs in vertebrates have tended to exclude motor neurons as members of the CPG, with most oscillatory function attributed to interneurons (Kiehn, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kiehn, 2016.

claim: Leech excitatory motor neurons have not been shown to be members of the swim CPG, as injection of a pulse of current fails to reset the cycle phase.
source: Leech excitatory motor neurons have not been shown to be members of the swim CPG, as injection of a pulse of current fails to reset the cycle phase (Kristan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kristan et al., 2005.

claim: Leech inhibitory motor neurons are ascribed a role in swimming rhythm generation using the phase-resetting criterion.
source: However, leech inhibitory motor neurons are ascribed a role in swimming rhythm generation using the phase-resetting criterion (Mullins et al., 2011), motor neurons comprise the crab stomatogastric CPG (Marder and Bucher, 2007), and recent work has shown that motor neurons are key components of several locomotory pattern generators.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mullins et al., 2011 and Marder and Bucher, 2007.

claim: Motor neurons comprise the crab stomatogastric CPG.
source: However, leech inhibitory motor neurons are ascribed a role in swimming rhythm generation using the phase-resetting criterion (Mullins et al., 2011), motor neurons comprise the crab stomatogastric CPG (Marder and Bucher, 2007), and recent work has shown that motor neurons are key components of several locomotory pattern generators.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Marder and Bucher, 2007.

claim: Recent work has shown that motor neurons are key components of several locomotory pattern generators.
source: However, leech inhibitory motor neurons are ascribed a role in swimming rhythm generation using the phase-resetting criterion (Mullins et al., 2011), motor neurons comprise the crab stomatogastric CPG (Marder and Bucher, 2007), and recent work has shown that motor neurons are key components of several locomotory pattern generators.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the subsequent examples.

claim: In leech crawling, current pulses to the CV elongation motor neurons reset the phase of fictive crawling.
source: In leech crawling, which consists of cyclic elongation and contraction phases, current pulses to the CV elongation motor neurons do indeed reset the phase of fictive crawling.
evidence: This is a statement about leech crawling motor neurons.

claim: The CV neurons in leech crawling were not concluded to be necessary components of the CPG because tonic hyperpolarization failed to abolish the crawling rhythm.
source: However, the CV neurons were not concluded to be necessary components of the CPG because tonic hyperpolarization failed to abolish the crawling rhythm. Anatomical removal, arguably the more relevant test of necessity, was not reported (Rotstein et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rotstein et al., 2017.

claim: In zebrafish, motor neurons for swimming are bidirectionally coupled to locomotion-driving interneurons by gap junctions, and influence their recruitment, synaptic transmission, and firing frequency during locomotion.
source: In zebrafish, motor neurons for swimming are bidirectionally coupled to locomotion-driving interneurons by gap junctions, and influence their recruitment, synaptic transmission, and firing frequency during locomotion (Song et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Song et al., 2016.

claim: There is a growing recognition that motor neurons are not limited to conveying oscillatory signals from interneurons, but may themselves participate in rhythm generation.
source: Hence, there is a growing recognition that motor neurons are not limited to conveying oscillatory signals from interneurons, but may themselves participate in rhythm generation.
evidence: This is a general statement about the evolving understanding of motor neuron function.

claim: When the VNC and DNC of C. elegans were severed, independent, generally higher frequency undulations occurred posterior to the severed region.
source: One difference between our results and previous findings in leeches is in the effect of severing the VNC. When we severed the VNC and DNC of C. elegans, we found that independent, generally higher frequency undulations occurred posterior to the severed region (Figures 6 and 7).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Disruption of the leech VNC was not sufficient to prevent wave propagation from head to tail.
source: Disruption of the leech VNC, by contrast, was not sufficient to prevent wave propagation from head to tail (Yu et al., 1999), suggesting that proprioceptive information suffices to propagate the wave.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yu et al., 1999.

claim: Severing the VNC intersegmental coordinating neurons in in vitro leech preparations induced uncoordinated fictive swim oscillations at different frequencies occurring on either side of the cut.
source: However, severing the VNC intersegmental coordinating neurons in in vitro preparations induced uncoordinated fictive swim oscillations at different frequencies occurring on either side of the cut (Weeks, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Weeks, 1981.

claim: The laser lesioning of the VNC likely did not remove the severed processes of premotor interneurons.
